name: Margaret Fenwick
presenting_complaint: Persistent inpatient hyperglycaemia (BGL 19 mmol/L) on the surgical ward

medical_history.social: Retired teacher. Non-smoker. Independent at home.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 68-year-old woman admitted with community-acquired pneumonia has persistent hyperglycaemia (BGL 19.2 mmol/L) despite her usual oral agents. She has type 2 diabetes and was started on prednisolone 25 mg daily this admission. She remains on metformin and empagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor). She is eating and drinking. Obs: BP 132/78, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 97%, afebrile.
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the treating RMO, including a safe inpatient insulin plan.

subjective: Diabetes history: type, duration, HbA1c, usual regimen, hypoglycaemia awareness and any prior DKA
Identify drivers of hyperglycaemia this admission: corticosteroid (prednisolone), acute infection/illness, reduced mobility
Oral intake, fasting status and any planned procedures/imaging with contrast
Symptoms of DKA/HHS (polyuria, thirst, nausea, abdominal pain) and screen for ketones given SGLT2 use; document allergies
objective: Chart formal BGL monitoring (e.g. QID: pre-meal and pre-bed, plus a night check while on steroids)
Bedside capillary/blood ketones given SGLT2 inhibitor and acute illness (euglycaemic DKA can occur with normal glucose)
Review UEC/eGFR (metformin and contrast safety) and current observations/temperature for ongoing sepsis
Assess for volume status and any evidence of intercurrent deterioration
assessment: Inpatient/stress + steroid-induced hyperglycaemia in established type 2 diabetes, driven by prednisolone and acute pneumonia
At risk of euglycaemic DKA while on an SGLT2 inhibitor during acute illness — this must be flagged
Poor baseline control (HbA1c 8.9%) requiring a proactive, not purely reactive, insulin plan
plan: Do NOT manage on a sliding-scale/correction-only regimen alone — prescribe a full BASAL-BOLUS-CORRECTION regimen: basal insulin (e.g. glargine ~0.2–0.3 units/kg nocte), prandial rapid-acting insulin (e.g. aspart) with meals, plus a correction scale for high readings
Continue the basal insulin even if the patient becomes fasting (never omit basal in type 1; keep basal going in insulin-requiring type 2)
WITHHOLD the SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) during this acute illness — euglycaemic DKA risk; document the reason and a plan to recommence when well
Anticipate steroid-induced hyperglycaemia: prednisolone in the morning causes afternoon/evening peaks — weight insulin accordingly and review daily as the steroid dose changes
Chart hypoglycaemia treatment orders (fast-acting carbohydrate if able to swallow; IV 10% glucose if not) and review/titrate the insulin daily against the BGL trend
Hold metformin around IV contrast and in any AKI; check renal function
Refer diabetes educator/dietitian; plan discharge medication reconciliation and GP handover of every change (including when to restart the SGLT2 inhibitor)

critical_errors: Leaving the SGLT2 inhibitor (empagliflozin) charted through an acute illness — precipitates euglycaemic DKA; it must be withheld during acute illness/surgery
Managing hyperglycaemia on a sliding scale (correction insulin) alone without a documented basal-bolus-correction regimen, or omitting basal insulin when the patient is fasting
Failing to check ketones/consider euglycaemic DKA in a symptomatic SGLT2-treated patient because the glucose looks acceptable
must_not_miss: Basal-bolus-correction regimen documented (not sliding scale alone)
SGLT2 inhibitor withheld during acute illness
Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia recognised and BGL monitoring plus hypoglycaemia orders charted
